title: Genotype replacement in R
text:
When a new genotype arrives, the share of sequences that belong to it often follows an S-shaped curve. A logistic model fitted to monthly sequence counts sums up the takeover in one number: how fast the odds of sampling the new genotype grow each month.
This tutorial uses simulated data, so you can check that the model recovers a known answer. You’ll need dplyr and ggplot2.

title: Genotype replacement in R
text:
1. Simulate sequence counts
Three years of monthly sequencing, about 40 sequences a month, with the new genotype reaching half of all sequences in month 18.

library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

set.seed(42)

months <- 0:35
true_growth <- 0.25

seqs <- tibble(
  month = months,
  n = rpois(length(months), 40),
  new = rbinom(length(months), n, plogis(true_growth * (months - 18))),
  old = n - new
)

head(seqs)

# A tibble: 6 × 4
  month     n   new   old
  <int> <int> <int> <int>
1     0    48     0    48
2     1    36     0    36
3     2    40     0    40
4     3    33     0    33
5     4    39     0    39
6     5    49     2    47

title: Genotype replacement in R
text:
2. Plot the raw proportions

ggplot(seqs, aes(month, new / n)) +
  geom_point(aes(size = n), colour = "#B2433A", alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3.5, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Proportion new genotype") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)




Share of sequences belonging to the new genotype each month. Point size shows the number of sequences.

title: Genotype replacement in R
text:
3. Fit a logistic model
A binomial GLM with month as the only predictor. The slope is the growth rate on the log-odds scale.

fit <- glm(cbind(new, old) ~ month, family = binomial, data = seqs)

coef(summary(fit))

              Estimate Std. Error   z value     Pr(>|z|)
(Intercept) -4.5876913 0.23203198 -19.77181 5.207782e-87
month        0.2516952 0.01222148  20.59449 3.075353e-94

title: Genotype replacement in R
text:
4. Plot the fit

pred <- predict(fit, se.fit = TRUE)

seqs <- seqs |>
  mutate(
    fit = plogis(pred$fit),
    lo = plogis(pred$fit - 1.96 * pred$se.fit),
    hi = plogis(pred$fit + 1.96 * pred$se.fit)
  )

ggplot(seqs, aes(month)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#B2433A", alpha = 0.18) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fit), colour = "#B2433A", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_point(aes(y = new / n, size = n), colour = "#1D2930", alpha = 0.55) +
  scale_size_area(max_size = 3.5, guide = "none") +
  labs(x = "Month", y = "Proportion new genotype") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)




Fitted logistic curve with a 95% confidence interval.

title: Genotype replacement in R
text:
5. Read off the growth advantage

growth <- coef(fit)[["month"]]

c(growth = growth, odds_ratio_per_month = exp(growth))

              growth odds_ratio_per_month 
           0.2516952            1.2862039 


The model estimates a growth rate of 0.25 per month against a true value of 0.25. Each month, the odds that a sequence belongs to the new genotype multiply by about 1.29.






NoteWith real data



Sequencing is rarely random. Check how samples were chosen for sequencing before reading the slope as a fitness advantage, and if you pool several places, consider a random effect for location.

title: Dengue: a primer
text:
At a glance

Family

Flaviviridae, genus Orthoflavivirus

Genome

About 10.7 kb of positive-sense, single-stranded RNA

Serotypes

Four: DENV-1, DENV-2, DENV-3 and DENV-4

Vectors

Aedes aegypti, and Ae. albopictus in some settings

Burden

An estimated 100–400 million infections a year, with about half the world’s population at risk (WHO)

title: Dengue: a primer
text:
The virus
The genome is translated as a single polyprotein, then cut into three structural proteins (capsid, prM and envelope) and seven non-structural proteins (NS1, NS2A, NS2B, NS3, NS4A, NS4B and NS5). The envelope (E) gene was the classic target for genotyping. Whole genomes are now routine.

title: Dengue: a primer
text:
Serotypes, genotypes and lineages
Infection with one serotype gives long-lasting protection against that serotype, but cross-protection against the others is short-lived. A second infection with a different serotype carries a higher risk of severe dengue.
Each serotype splits into genotypes. DENV-2, for example, has the Asian I, Asian II, Asian-American, American, Cosmopolitan and sylvatic genotypes. A lineage nomenclature now divides genotypes further, which makes surveillance reports easier to compare.

title: Dengue: a primer
text:
Transmission
Aedes aegypti lives close to people, bites during the day and breeds in small containers of water, which makes dengue an urban disease. Ae. albopictus tolerates cooler climates and is behind the occasional local transmission now seen in southern Europe. Temperature affects how long mosquitoes live and how quickly the virus develops inside them, so climate shapes when and where outbreaks happen.

title: Dengue: a primer
text:
How my work fits in
My DPhil looks at how DENV-2 genotypes replace one another in Vietnam, and at the global spread of the DENV-2 Cosmopolitan genotype after the COVID-19 pandemic. More on the research page.

title: Dengue: a primer
text:
Resources


WHO fact sheet: dengue and severe dengue
Nextstrain dengue builds: real-time phylogenies by serotype
Dengue lineage nomenclature
OpenDengue: global case counts in one dataset



Next: Genotype replacement in R, a hands-on tutorial with simulated sequence data.

title: Streptococcus intermedius: a primer
text:
At a glance

Group

Streptococcus anginosus group, with S. anginosus and S. constellatus

Gram stain

Gram-positive cocci in chains

Habitat

Normal flora of the mouth, upper airway, gut and genitourinary tract

Known for

Abscesses, especially in the brain and liver

Key toxin

Intermedilysin, which targets human cells through CD59

title: Streptococcus intermedius: a primer
text:
The organism
Older papers call this group the “Streptococcus milleri group”. Lancefield grouping is unreliable here: isolates can carry group A, C, F or G antigens, or none. On culture, the group is often described as smelling of caramel. Identification now relies on MALDI-TOF or sequencing, because biochemical tests struggle to separate the three species.

title: Streptococcus intermedius: a primer
text:
Why it matters clinically
All three species can cause invasive infection, but S. intermedius is the one most often linked to brain and liver abscesses. Brain abscesses often have a dental or sinus source.

title: Streptococcus intermedius: a primer
text:
Intermedilysin
Intermedilysin is a cholesterol-dependent cytolysin, a pore-forming toxin. Most toxins in this family bind cholesterol on any cell, but intermedilysin first binds human CD59, so it damages human cells far more readily than those of other animals.

title: Streptococcus intermedius: a primer
text:
Resources


From normal flora to brain abscesses: a review of Streptococcus intermedius (Frontiers in Microbiology, 2020)

title: Research
text: I turn pathogen genomes and surveillance data into evidence for public health: where infections come from, how they spread once they arrive, and how genomic surveillance should be designed to answer those questions. Below are the main findings from my published work, with figures and links to each paper. Work still in preparation is marked as such.

title: Research
text:
Dengue genotype dynamics
Each of dengue’s four serotypes is made up of genotypes that rise and fall. I use phylogenetics and phylodynamics to work out where new genotypes come from, how they spread, and why some replace those already circulating.

What we found

Among dengue patients sampled at the Hospital for Tropical Diseases in Ho Chi Minh City, DENV-2 replaced DENV-1 as the predominant serotype in 2019, with several DENV-2 genotypes circulating side by side.
The Cosmopolitan genotype re-emerged through at least three separate recent introductions into southern Vietnam (clades A, B and C), sharing ancestry with sequences from Indonesia (A and B) and Cambodia (C).
Two of these clades had persisted locally for at least five years, roughly two years before they were first sampled, suggesting undetected transmission across several dengue seasons.

Tran, Inward et al., Emerging Infectious Diseases 2023 (joint first author)


Now working on

How introduction, establishment and amplification shape the replacement of DENV-2 genotypes in Vietnam
The global expansion of the DENV-2 Cosmopolitan genotype after the COVID-19 pandemic, with selection analyses across the genome
How dengue lineages spread and become established across Southeast Asia, combining phylogeography with environmental suitability modelling



Dengue primer · Genotype replacement tutorial

title: Research
section: How variants were introduced and spread
text:
How variants were introduced and spread
Before my DPhil I worked on how SARS-CoV-2 variants of concern arrived in England and what drove their spread once they were there.



Omicron BA.1

Analysing 115,622 genomes, we identified more than 6,000 separate introductions of Omicron BA.1 into England.
Six of the eight largest lineages were already spreading when Omicron was first reported on 22 November 2021, and importation continued despite travel restrictions because well-connected countries elsewhere were exporting it.
About 6% of introductions accounted for about 80% of BA.1 infections reported in England up to the end of January 2022.

Tsui, McCrone, Lambert, Bajaj, Inward, Bosetti et al., Science 2023 (joint first author)




Delta

Delta was introduced into England an estimated minimum of 1,458 times, and about half of these introductions (56.5%) came from India.
After hotel quarantine began, the share of introductions from India that led to onward transmission in England fell from 37.7% to 26.9%.
Once Delta was established, faster spread was associated with local population mixing rather than with the number of new importations.

McCrone, Hill, Bajaj et al., Nature 2022





The largest Omicron BA.1 transmission lineage spreading out of Greater London, 30 November to 20 December 2021, reconstructed by continuous phylogeography. Adapted (cropped) from Tsui, McCrone, Lambert, Bajaj, Inward, Bosetti et al., Science 2023 (author manuscript, CC BY 4.0).


Also: lineage dynamics in Mexico (eLife 2023, joint first author) and Chile (PNAS Nexus 2024).

title: Research
text:
Designing genomic surveillance
Which genomes get sequenced, and how cases are reported, shapes what surveillance data can tell us. Getting this right matters most where surveillance resources are limited.



Sampling genomes

How sequences are chosen changes estimates of Rt and the growth rate, while R0 and the estimated date an outbreak began stay relatively stable.
In Hong Kong, sampling sequences in proportion to weekly case numbers matched case-based Rt most closely. In Amazonas, Brazil, opportunistic sampling gave the estimates that differed most.
Molecular clock dating placed the emergence of the Gamma variant in Amazonas in late October to early November 2020, about five weeks before the first reported case.

Inward, Parag & Faria, Nature Communications 2022 (first author) · Code




Reporting delays

Reporting delays varied markedly between states and over time in Argentina, Brazil, Colombia and Mexico.
Changing the geographical scale of the analysis shifted estimates of how fast cases were growing by up to 0.13 per day.
Applying national-level corrections to a single state could mislead: in Roraima, Brazil, the epidemic appeared to have stabilised while cases were still changing substantially.

Inward, Jackson et al., Epidemics 2022 (joint first author)





Hong Kong, early 2020: Rt estimated from genomes (BDSKY, blue) and from cases (EpiFilter, green), using all available sequences (left) and sequences sampled in proportion to cases (right). Adapted (cropped) from Inward, Parag & Faria, Nature Communications 2022 (CC BY 4.0).

title: Research
text:
Chikungunya transmission and climate
I model chikungunya outbreaks in France and Brazil with renewal equations and generalised additive models, to separate the roles of climate, importation and immunity in each setting, and use climate counterfactuals to ask how much climate shaped transmission.

In preparation
Manuscript in preparation. I presented this work as a poster at the International Pandemic Sciences Conference in Singapore in 2026.

title: Research
text:
Reproducible pipelines
GRAPEVNE is a graphical environment for building and sharing analysis pipelines in infectious disease research, and a chapter of my thesis. I write my own genomic workflows (alignment, tree building, dating and selection analyses) as Snakemake pipelines so others can rerun them.

What we built

GRAPEVNE: an open-source platform for building modular analysis pipelines through a graphical interface, shaped by consulting about 50 infectious disease modellers, bioinformaticians and genomic epidemiologists.
Our dengue pipeline automates the whole process from retrieving sequences to phylogeographic inference, and can be shared without revealing the underlying data.
DART: an open pipeline that brings climate, socio-economic and population data together for disease modelling. It can run locally, so surveillance data need not leave the country, and was demonstrated on dengue in Vietnam.

title: Research
text:
Field epidemiology
Since September 2026 I’ve been a fellow on the UK Field Epidemiology Training Programme, based at UKHSA’s North West Field Service in Liverpool. It is a two-year, full-time fellowship run by UKHSA and accredited by TEPHINET.
Fellows learn on the job across outbreak investigation, surveillance, applied research, scientific communication and teaching. The programme also supports UKHSA’s international outbreak response and capacity building, which is where I want to connect genomic epidemiology with public health practice.

Field epidemiology · Genomic surveillance · Arboviruses



I’m a field epidemiology fellow with the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) and a final-year DPhil candidate at the University of Oxford. title: Chikungunya: a primer
text:
At a glance

Family

Togaviridae, genus Alphavirus

Genome

About 11.8 kb of positive-sense, single-stranded RNA

Lineages

West African, East/Central/South African (ECSA) and Asian, plus the Indian Ocean lineage that emerged from ECSA

Vectors

Aedes aegypti and Ae. albopictus

Disease

Sudden fever and severe joint pain, which can last for months (WHO)

title: Chikungunya: a primer
text:
The virus
The genome carries two open reading frames. The first encodes four non-structural proteins (nsP1–nsP4) that copy the genome. The second encodes the structural proteins: capsid, E3, E2, 6K/TF and E1.

title: Chikungunya: a primer
text:
Lineages and adaptation
During the 2005–06 outbreak on La Réunion, an alanine-to-valine change at position 226 of the E1 protein (E1-A226V) let some ECSA strains spread more efficiently in Ae. albopictus. That mosquito is now established across much of southern Europe, which is one reason chikungunya can transmit locally there.

title: Chikungunya: a primer
text:
Where it spreads
The Asian lineage reached the Americas in late 2013, and the ECSA lineage was detected in Brazil the following year. Outbreaks with local transmission have also occurred in Italy and France.

title: Chikungunya: a primer
text:
How my work fits in
I model chikungunya outbreaks in France and Brazil with renewal equations, and use climate counterfactuals to ask how much climate shaped transmission. The renewal-equation tutorial walks through the core idea.

title: Estimating Rt with a renewal equation
text:
The renewal equation says that new infections today depend on recent infections, weighted by the generation interval \(w_s\), the chance that \(s\) days separate an infection from the one it causes:
\[
I_t \sim \text{Poisson}\left(R_t \sum_{s \geq 1} I_{t-s}\, w_s\right)
\]
This tutorial simulates an outbreak with a known \(R_t\), then estimates it back with the approach of Cori et al. (2013), written out in base R so every step is visible. You’ll need ggplot2 for the plots.

title: Estimating Rt with a renewal equation
text:
1. Set up the generation interval
A gamma distribution with a mean of six days, cut at three weeks.

library(ggplot2)

set.seed(1)

days <- 1:120
w <- dgamma(1:21, shape = 6, rate = 1)
w <- w / sum(w)

infectiousness <- function(inc, t) {
  s <- 1:min(t - 1, length(w))
  sum(inc[t - s] * w[s])
}

title: Estimating Rt with a renewal equation
text:
2. Simulate an outbreak
\(R_t\) is 1.5 until day 50, when a control measure brings it down to 0.8.

rt_true <- ifelse(days < 50, 1.5, 0.8)

inc <- numeric(length(days))
inc[1:5] <- 5

for (t in 6:length(days)) {
  inc[t] <- rpois(1, rt_true[t] * infectiousness(inc, t))
}

ggplot(data.frame(day = days, cases = inc), aes(day, cases)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#9A6714", width = 0.85) +
  labs(x = "Day", y = "Cases") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)




Simulated daily incidence.

title: Estimating Rt with a renewal equation
section: 3. Estimate Rt over a sliding window
text:
3. Estimate Rt over a sliding window
With a gamma prior on \(R_t\) (shape \(a\), scale \(b\)) and a window of \(\tau\) days, the posterior is also gamma, with shape \(a + \sum I_t\) and rate \(1/b + \sum \Lambda_t\), where \(\Lambda_t\) is the total infectiousness on day \(t\).

tau <- 7
a <- 1
b <- 5

lambda <- c(0, sapply(2:length(days), \(t) infectiousness(inc, t)))

est <- data.frame(day = 15:length(days))
est$shape <- sapply(est$day, \(t) a + sum(inc[(t - tau + 1):t]))
est$rate <- sapply(est$day, \(t) 1 / b + sum(lambda[(t - tau + 1):t]))
est$mean <- est$shape / est$rate
est$lo <- qgamma(0.025, est$shape, est$rate)
est$hi <- qgamma(0.975, est$shape, est$rate)

title: Estimating Rt with a renewal equation
text:
4. Compare with the truth

ggplot(est, aes(day)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 1, colour = "grey60", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#9A6714", alpha = 0.25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = mean), colour = "#9A6714", linewidth = 0.9) +
  geom_step(data = data.frame(day = days, rt = rt_true), aes(y = rt), linetype = "dashed", colour = "#1D2930") +
  labs(x = "Day", y = expression(R[t])) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 13)




Estimated Rt with a 95% credible interval. The dashed line is the true value.




The estimate tracks the true \(R_t\) and takes about a window’s length to catch up after the drop on day 50.






NoteFor mosquito-borne viruses



The generation interval for dengue or chikungunya includes the time the virus spends developing inside the mosquito, so it is longer than for a respiratory virus and changes with temperature. Imported cases also need separating from local ones, or they inflate \(R_t\). See the chikungunya primer.
